title: The Oakmere Will
logline: A captain long believed dead comes home to find his great-uncle's farm signed away to a cousin he has never trusted, and the only people who can prove the will a fraud are an apothecary's dispensing book and a letter that never reached him.
promise: The rightful heir gets his farm back, the fraud is exposed without a drop of blood spilled, and the woman who grieved him in silence is finally asked properly.
setting: Amberlight parish and the Winchester road, October 1816

cast.name: Miss Judith Vane
cast.station: keeps house for her brother, the apothecary; no fortune of her own
cast.want: to see the truth of the will established before an honest man is cheated of everything
cast.appearance: Fair, freckled, of middling height, with reddish hair she cannot keep pinned and a habit of looking directly at whoever is speaking.
cast.dress: Sprigged muslin in summer, a grey wool pelisse in winter, both mended with more thrift than skill.
cast.voice_note: quiet, precise, says less than she is thinking

cast.name: Mr Silas Rowe
cast.station: curate of Amberlight; eighty a year and no expectations
cast.want: to help without making the matter worse through his own clumsiness
cast.appearance: Tall and thin, dark hair worn slightly too long, with the stoop of a man used to low doorways and a face that gives away more than he intends.
cast.dress: Worn black coat, carefully brushed, and linen that has been turned at the cuffs.
cast.voice_note: earnest, over-explains, trails off when he loses his nerve

cast.name: Mrs Honoria Pike
cast.station: widow of a naval surgeon; three hundred a year and a house on the green
cast.want: to be the first in the parish to know how the will affair ends, and to take some credit for the outcome
cast.appearance: Short and broad, with grey hair pinned severely under a lace cap, and small quick eyes set in a round weathered face.
cast.dress: Black bombazine with a plain white fichu, ten years out of fashion and immaculately kept.
cast.voice_note: brisk, delighted by her own certainty, interrupts

cast.name: Captain Nathaniel Farr
cast.station: half-pay officer, presumed heir to Oakmere Farm, worth some three hundred a year
cast.want: to reclaim the home and the promise his great-uncle made him before he went for a soldier
cast.appearance: weathered and lean, sun-darkened where an Englishman is usually pale, with a slight limp and a scar along one hand.
cast.dress: a faded regimental coat at first, plain and unmarked of rank, worn thin at the cuffs.
cast.voice_note: spare, direct, softens only when speaking of the farm or of Judith

cast.name: Mr Vernon Hartwell
cast.station: Fenner's cousin's son, presently in possession of Oakmere under a disputed will
cast.want: to secure the farm and its rents before his debts in town come due
cast.appearance: fair-haired and soft-handed, a little too well dressed for a working farm, with a smile that arrives before it is warranted.
cast.dress: a town-tailored coat and polished boots wholly unsuited to mud, a watch-chain worn where it can be seen.
cast.voice_note: smooth, quick to reassure, never quite answers the question

cast.name: Mrs Dorcas Whitlow
cast.station: housekeeper at Oakmere Farm these thirty years, dependent on her place
cast.want: to keep her position and not be blamed for what she saw the day the will was signed
cast.appearance: grey-haired under a plain cap, stooped, with work-roughened hands never quite still.
cast.dress: a dark stuff gown, a clean apron, a ring of keys at her waist.
cast.voice_note: hesitant, drops her voice when frightened, speaks in short bursts

cast.name: Mr Owen Vane
cast.station: apothecary of Amberlight; modest income from his shop
cast.want: to be believed by the gentry without being made to quarrel with them
cast.appearance: slight, bespectacled, with herb stains permanently on his cuffs and an ink-stained thumb.
cast.dress: a plain brown coat, often still in his apothecary's apron when called upon suddenly.
cast.voice_note: careful, exact with dates and numbers, uneasy outside his shop

chapters.title: The Coach on Friday
beats: Mrs Pike brings word to the circulating library that old Mr Aldous Fenner of Oakmere Farm has died a fortnight since.
She reports that his cousin's son, Mr Vernon Hartwell, has already moved into the farmhouse under a will drawn up only weeks before Fenner's death.
Judith Vane observes that the will cuts out Fenner's great-nephew, Captain Nathaniel Farr, believed killed abroad three years since.
Mrs Pike declares the captain certainly dead, since no letter has come from him in all that time.
The Friday coach draws up at the Bell, and a sun-browned stranger steps down asking the way to Oakmere Farm — Captain Farr himself, very much alive.

chapters.title: Oakmere Farm
beats: Farr walks the mile to Oakmere and finds smoke rising from the chimney and unfamiliar curtains in windows he remembers as his great-uncle's.
Hartwell greets him civilly from the doorstep but does not ask him in, calling his arrival a surprise rather than a homecoming.
Hartwell produces the later will, drawn weeks before Fenner's death and witnessed by two of the farm's own servants, leaving everything to himself.
Farr states that his great-uncle promised him the farm by word before he went for a soldier, and has no paper to prove it.
Turned from his own door, Farr walks back toward the village, watched from an upstairs window by the housekeeper, Mrs Whitlow, who says nothing.

chapters.title: The Dispensing Book
beats: Lodging at the Bell on credit he can ill afford, Farr seeks out Judith Vane, who knew him before he went to war.
Judith takes him to her brother Owen's shop, where Owen is reluctant to be drawn into a quarrel with gentry.
Owen consults his dispensing book and finds the entry for the very date the will was signed.
The entry shows Fenner was given a heavy dose against pain that same morning, and Owen recalls the old man could scarcely say his own name that day.
Judith concludes that a dispensing book alone will not answer, and that they need someone who was inside Oakmere on the day of the signing.

chapters.title: What Mrs Whitlow Knew
beats: Judith and Mr Rowe call at Oakmere under pretence of parish almsgiving, and are received stiffly by Hartwell in the hall.
Alone with Whitlow in the kitchen, Judith learns the housekeeper was told exactly what account to give of the day of the signing.
Whitlow admits, her voice dropping, that months before the death she wrote herself to Farr's regiment warning that his great-uncle was failing.
She recalls handing that letter to Hartwell to go with the rest of the post, since he had by then taken charge of it.
Frightened at having said so much, Whitlow cannot say whether the letter was ever sent at all.

chapters.title: The Road to Winchester
beats: Judith carries Owen's dispensing book and Whitlow's account to Farr at the Bell.
Farr resolves to lay the evidence before the Winchester attorney who holds Fenner's papers.
Mr Rowe warns that Farr alone would be taken for a fortune hunter telling a convenient story, and proposes Judith go too, with the book in her own keeping.
Judith agrees, over Mrs Pike's loud objections about a lady travelling with a strange captain.
A few miles short of Winchester a wheel gives way on their hired chaise, and the driver says no other conveyance will pass before morning.

chapters.title: The Wayside House
beats: Stranded at a farmhouse by the road while a wheelwright is fetched, Farr tells Judith what became of him after the battle that was reported his death.
He describes a year in a foreign hospital, and letters gone astray once his regiment moved on without a fixed direction for him.
Judith admits, for the first time, that she had heard him reported dead and grieved it more than she let the parish see.
Working through the dates together by the fire, they realize Whitlow's letter, if it was ever sent, would have passed through Hartwell's own hands first.
They agree that Hartwell alone had both the means and the reason to see that letter never leave the house.

chapters.title: The Attorney's Pigeonhole
beats: In Winchester the next morning, the attorney confirms that the earlier will naming Farr was never formally revoked, only set aside as superseded.
He permits Judith and Farr to search a shelf of unclaimed correspondence kept at his office for want of a clear direction.
Among the letters they find Whitlow's own, misdirected there through a clerk's error rather than destroyed.
Its date proves that Fenner was already failing months before Hartwell's will was ever drawn up.
The attorney agrees to summon Hartwell to account, and Farr and Judith hurry back toward Amberlight before he can sell off the farm's stock.

chapters.title: Oakmere Reclaimed
beats: Before Whitlow and Rowe as witnesses, Farr and Judith lay out the dispensing book, the housekeeper's account, and the recovered letter.
Hartwell cannot account for the letter's date, nor explain why it never left the house.
With the attorney's authority behind them, Hartwell quits Oakmere before nightfall rather than face a suit.
Mrs Pike carries the whole affair through the parish within a day, casting herself as the one who first doubted the will.
Confirmed at last in his inheritance, Farr asks Judith what he could not honestly have asked her with nothing to his name, and she accepts.
